extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and readers of architectural theory/criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for designing, carving, finishing, and valuing architectural ornament and the memorial function of buildings, with emphasis on hand-work, variation, proportion, and permanence. Includes stylistic and moral criteria for domestic and civic architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and vertical/lateral division
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful proportional relationships govern shafts, arches, and stories (e.g., the lower shafts, upper shafts, and wall being severally expressed by a, b, and c, then a:c::c:b; upper and lower shaft diameters related so that one upper is placed above one below, and the upper story adds a third term in its pinnacles). Lateral divisions diminish in regular or alternating order (seven arches in the lower story diminish a, c, b, d; upper story five arches diminish similarly), securing an overall pyramidal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportional rules and graduated diminution to achieve harmonious vertical and lateral composition; avoid placing shafts of upper arches directly over those of the lower; treat the whole façade as a pyramidal ensemble. Examples from Byzantine façades and descriptions of seven- and five-arch arrangements illustrate the intended relationships. The numerical ratios and stepwise diminution should be used to preserve the sense of order while allowing other variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate asymmetry and effective symmetry by variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Builders often employed purposeful variations in dimensions and ordering rather than strict repetition — northern and southern arches may differ notably in width and cornice height; apparently symmetrical members are frequently not truly symmetrical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should favor subtle, controlled variations over rigid, mechanical symmetry to produce life and movement in a façade. The examples of the Cathedral of Bayeux and Abbeville show large and small intentional departures from measurement that serve visual vitality rather than being errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety over mechanical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in size, shape, and decoration are not blunders but deliberate rejections of exact measurement in favour of an organic, nature-like variety. The medieval architect's 'fixed scorn' or 'dislike' of accuracy in measurements can be an aesthetic principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate precision of measurement with correctness of design; where appropriate, introduce variations that mimic natural irregularities to achieve effective symmetry and visual richness. Recognize when departures from measurement serve unity rather than harm it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality of assimilation (use of available materials and sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty which turns all available material to its purposes — the architect adopting shapes and motifs from any humble or miscellaneous source and persisting in combining them to produce a harmonious whole (example: arcade columns of Ferrara; prototype found in awning rack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to adopt ideas from diverse, even lowly, sources with humility and boldness. Successful assimilation requires intelligence and feeling so that disparate elements can be integrated into an ecclesiastical or civic harmony rather than pasted ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-work and the life of the hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-work can be distinguished from machine-work by pauses, varied handling, and evidence of care — the hand puts heart into detail producing accents and life. Machine-work tends to uniformity and 'the look of equal trouble everywhere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer and preserve skilled hand-work where the craftsman’s thought and feeling are evident. Allow visible variation (pauses, stronger and lighter strikes) so parts set off one another; avoid machine-produced regularity that kills vitality. Where men work heartily, even imperfect workmanship will possess value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right finish vs. cold or mechanical finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Right finish is the full rendering of the intended impression; high finish renders a well-intended and vivid impression. Cold cutting or uniformly even finishing — 'the smooth, diffused tranquillity of heartless pains' — kills life. High polish mistaken for completeness produces dead work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a finish that conveys the intended expression rather than mechanical perfection. Rougher, more expressive handling often achieves more life than over-smoothing. Avoid equating completeness with gloss or uniform polish attainable by sandpaper or engine-lathe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture as chisel-painting; virtue of incompletion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture is not merely cutting the true form but cutting the effect of it: chisels 'paint' with light and shadow. Often incomplete or seemingly rude touches (incompleteness) achieve deeper expression than literal, fully realized form (examples: Mino da Fiesole, certain child-figures, and sacristy statues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective finishing and unconventional touches to create lines of light and spots of darkness; allow intentional incompleteness where it increases expressiveness. Do not attempt always to reproduce the literal 'true' form in marble or stone if a partial, painted-with-chisel approach better serves the impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be executed with enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: The central question regarding ornament: 'Was it done with enjoyment — was the carver happy while he was about it?' If the workman hated the work, the ornament will be dead; life cannot be bought by money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure craftsmen engage genuinely and delightedly with their work; value artisans who take pleasure in carving. Recognize that paid, resentful, or hurried labour produces lifeless ornament. Patronage and procurement should not substitute money for care and joy in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap imitation and machine ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Stamped metals, artificial stones, imitation woods and bronzes, cast-iron work, and other cheap, short, or easy modes of ornament are obstacles that make work shallower and colder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eschew mass-produced or imitation ornamentation in favour of authentic hand-made detail; where appropriate, explore geometric color-mosaic as a rich alternative that does not rely on machine stamping. Doing without machine ornament and cast substitutes is advocated as within our power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory as a primary function of Architecture (the Sixth Lamp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture centralizes and protects sacred influence of memory: it helps men remember what writing and poetry cannot; there are two duties — render present architecture historical, and preserve the architecture of past ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design civic and domestic buildings with an eye to their potential as memorials: build in stability and metaphorical or historical meaning so they may serve future remembrance. Prioritize durability and meaningful decoration that will communicate across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic buildings should be built to last (houses as temples)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an evil sign when houses are built to last one generation only. A good man's house is a sanctuary that should endure, producing a warm monument in the hearth and home rather than ephemeral tenements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor construction and design choices that grant permanence, continuity, and sanctity to domestic architecture. Resist fashions and economic impulses that produce thin, tottering, foundationless shells; aim for dwellings that can be venerated by descendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail variation and individuality in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Small-scale variations — unequal quatrefoils, arcs that are not perfect semicircles, rhomboid bases, and hundreds of distinct animal carvings as fillers — generate grace and evidence of thoughtfulness and fancy. The multitude of differing small elements contributes to the overall vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making repetitive small panels uniformly equal; vary shapes and motifs across repetitive modules so that the eye perceives variety and inventiveness. Use individually thought details (each animal different, arcs adjusted to space) to give richness even in large quantities of ornament.
